check: the sampling interval stretched to 65 seconds on one reading, which needed explaining rather than noting
why: The interval is nominally 600 ticks, about 30 seconds. A single 65-second gap could mean the server was falling behind, which precedes a stalled run, or it could be the profile's normal load oscillation. Distinguishing them matters because one is a warning and the other is the design.

whatTheDistributionShows.shape: bimodal: 24 samples at 27 to 31 seconds, and 15 stretched to 53 to 80 seconds
whatTheDistributionShows.interpretation: Two regimes rather than a drift. The nominal regime means the server is keeping the 20 ticks per second pace; the stretched one means it is not, which is what a deliberately overloaded server does.

theLagRateRisesButDoesNotDrift.naiveConclusion: The rate increased by 43 percent, which would suggest degradation.
theLagRateRisesButDoesNotDrift.segmentComparison: Segment 1 ran 42 per hour and segment 34 ran 42 per hour; segment 2 ran 71 and segment 35 ran 81. Fourteen hours apart, the same positions in the cycle give the same rates.
theLagRateRisesButDoesNotDrift.correctConclusion: The rate oscillates with the workload cycle rather than trending upward. The whole-run average differs between the two readings only because each covers a different mix of cycle phases.

whyTheRefillCadenceIsTheStrongerSignal: Refill intervals stayed between 17 and 22 minutes across segments 31 to 36, the same band as segments 1 to 6. A server genuinely falling behind would slow its refills too; a flat refill cadence alongside an oscillating lag rate is steady state under load.
recordOfMyOwnCaution: This is the third time this session that a whole-window average disagreed with the segmented view, after the build-interference and sampling-cadence cases. The pattern is consistent: the average hides the cycle, and the cycle is the finding.
